segments.say: So far this week we have used somebody else's idea of how to coordinate agents. Claude Code's agent teams are a good idea, and they did real work yesterday. But you should never be in a position where the only orchestrator you can use is one that somebody ships you. So the question for this lecture is not which orchestrator is best. It is: how much of one is there, actually. Ask it. And read the answer carefully, because it is refreshingly unglamorous. With the Agent SDK this is genuinely small: a function that maps your list of pieces onto calls, one prompt per item, fired concurrently with a cap so you do not launch forty at once, each one wrapped so that a single failure does not sink the batch, and the results collected through a typed tool call rather than scraped out of free text. Fifty to a hundred lines. Not a framework. And then the honest part, which is the tradeoff. What agent teams give you beyond that list is phased pipelines, adversarial verification passes, resumable runs, isolation between workers — and if you write your own, you are signing up to build every one of those yourself the day you need it. For a genuinely independent, fire-and-collect list of jobs, you need none of them. That is the real answer to when should I roll my own, and nobody in a launch video ever gives it to you.

Every tool in this space is sold to you as a category. Once you know the category is a hundred lines, you can ask a much better question, which is what the extra ten thousand lines in somebody else's are buying, and whether you need any of it this month. So let us write it. And watch what I put in this instruction, because most of it is not about orchestration at all. Write it as a JavaScript file using the Agent SDK. Then the part that matters: I know that makes it this project's first dependency, and I know the memory file says zero dependencies — that is a deliberate exception for a tool, not for the application, so install it, and write the exception down in the memory file. If you do not say that, one of two bad things happens. Either it refuses, correctly, because you told it a rule; or it quietly breaks the rule and you find out in three weeks. Naming the exception out loud is how a convention stays alive while still bending when it should. Then three real tasks against this repository, so that running it actually does something rather than printing hello three times. Look at what they are: a README for the tools folder, a short contributing note, a docs page describing the simulated data. Three jobs that touch nothing the others touch — the only shape this design is safe for. Every agent pinned to the sonnet model explicitly, because a tool that spawns agents is a tool that spends money and you should always know which model it is spending it on. Keep it readable — I want to be able to explain every line. And finally: do not ask me questions; if a choice comes up, make it, and tell me what you chose. That last line is there for a reason I learned the hard way. The first time I filmed this lecture, the agent did the responsible thing: it stopped and asked me whether a Python file really belonged in a Node project. A perfectly good question — and because I was not sitting there, it waited, and the whole take was wasted. An agent that stops to ask you something is an agent that is not working. So when you are going to walk away, either be there to answer, or say in the instruction that you will not be, and take responsibility for the choice it makes instead. One more clause worth stealing: if evidence is missing, say so rather than guess. What you must not do is leave the question open and assume.

Four sentences, none of them about orchestration, and between them they decide whether the thing that comes out is a tool you can run unattended or a script that stops halfway waiting for somebody who has gone to lunch. Now watch what it does before it writes a single line, because this is the part that separates a working script from a plausible one. It checks the repository layout. It installs the SDK. And then it opens the SDK's own type definitions on disk and reads them, so that it is not guessing at option names — which is exactly the failure mode you get when a model writes against a library from memory and invents a parameter that looks right and does not exist. The file it opens is sdk dot d dot ts, inside node modules, and then it checks the package's own entry points to see what is actually exported. Then it notices something nobody told it: there is no API key in this environment, but there is a Claude binary on the path, so the authentication will come from there instead. It confirmed that against the installed package rather than assuming it. If you want one habit to take from this whole week, it is that one — check the thing in front of you before you write code against it. The counter under the spinner is the evidence: four thousand tokens read, then nearly twelve thousand, and the file still does not exist. And notice how much of this is reading rather than typing. Of the two and a half minutes it spends here, almost all of it goes on establishing what is true, and a few seconds on the file. That ratio is not a quirk of this run. It is what competent work looks like when the typing is free: the expensive part stops being the writing and becomes the knowing what to write, which is exactly the shift this whole week has been about. And there is a specific reason reading the type definitions matters more with a library like this one than with almost anything else. The Agent SDK is new and it is moving. Anything written about it more than a couple of months ago is describing option names that may not exist any more. A model that answers from memory here is answering from a snapshot of a moving target. A model that opens the package on your disk is answering from the version you are actually going to run.

And here is what comes out. A constant naming the model, so the spend is never a mystery. A list of tasks. One function per task, each with its own brief and its own restricted tool list, all of them run concurrently, and a timed report at the end. That is the whole thing, and you could read it in a coffee break. One detail earns its place: each task's tool list is set twice — the tools the agent can see, and the tools already approved. That is what stops a headless run stalling on a permission prompt nobody is there to answer. Then it goes back and edits the memory file to record the exception, exactly as it was asked to. Read that diff, because it is a small masterpiece of not overreaching: zero dependencies for the application, one deliberate exception for a tool, and the reason spelled out — the running app still starts with no network and nothing beyond Node itself. The rule bent precisely as far as it needed to and no further, and the next person to open this repository will know why. That is worth pausing on, because a memory file that is never edited stops being a description of the project and becomes a wish. The useful version is the one that gets amended, in place, at the moment the exception is made — not the one that stays pristine while the code quietly drifts away from it. And look at what is not in the file, because that is the part people expect and do not find. There is no scheduler. There is no queue. There is no retry policy, no state machine, no plugin system. Concurrency is one cap on how many run at once. Failure handling is one wrapper per task. It also says what it did not verify. All three tasks succeeded, twenty two to seventy four seconds each. Cost it never checked — the result carries a total cost field it chose not to print. If you have been putting off writing something like this because you assumed it was an infrastructure project, this is the lecture where that assumption should die.

And now run it. This takes about a minute and a half, and there is nothing to look at while it does, because three agents are working at once and the report only prints when the last of them lands. The whole run is one line at a shell prompt, piped into tail, which is also why nothing appears until it is over. Three names print out of the tools folder, and then nothing at all. That silence is worth sitting through, because it is what an orchestrator actually looks like from the outside. No dashboard, no progress bars, no panes to cycle through. Three prompts went out at the same moment and three answers will come back, and in between there is genuinely nothing to see. Which is, if you think about it, the point. The whole reason to run work concurrently is so that you are not needed while it happens. A tool that gave you something to watch would be a tool asking for your attention, and your attention is the one thing this week has been trying to give back to you.

And here is the honest part. That run is piped into tail, and tail prints nothing at all until the thing feeding it exits - so three agents are working and the screen is a blank line with a cursor on it. There is nothing to watch, so we stop watching. Take the practical lesson with you: if you want to see a headless run while it happens, do not pipe it into tail. Stream it, or tee it into a file and follow the file instead. And then the last thing, which is the last thing after every build this week. A fresh session, and slash usage - because the only honest way to compare two ways of working is to know what each of them cost you.
